title: Third-Party KMS & HSM Integration Requirements for Private Deployments
author: Aisha Moore
body:
Summary:
This document defines Redwood Inference's minimum integration requirements, validation checklist, operational controls, and rollback procedures for third-party Key Management Systems (KMS) and Hardware Security Modules (HSM) used with Private deployments (VPC and on‑prem). It is intended for field engineers, SREs, and customers planning to bring their own key infrastructure or integrate a cloud KMS/HSM service.

Purpose and scope:
- Purpose: Ensure secure, auditable, and supportable key material management across private deployments while meeting regulatory constraints.
- Scope: Applies to any private deployment (VPC-hosted or on‑prem appliance) where customer-managed encryption keys are used for model artifacts, persistent KV caches, telemetry encryption, or secrets in the control plane. Excludes transient in-memory keys used only within process lifetimes.

Key objectives:
- Protect customer keys with FIPS 140-2/3 validated HSM or cloud KMS equivalents.
- Provide deterministic, testable integration steps that SRE and field teams can execute during onboarding.
- Define day‑2 operational guardrails (rotation, revocation, incident response) and safe rollback paths.

Requirements matrix (summary):
| Area | Minimum requirement | Rationale | Evidence for acceptance |
|---|---|---|---|
| KMS/HSM validation | FIPS 140-2 Level 2+ or cloud-managed equivalent (Azure Key Vault, AWS KMS, GCP KMS with CMEK) | Regulatory and integrity assurances | Certificate or attestation document; test provenance file |
| Key wrapping and envelope encryption | Support AES-256-GCM or AES-256-GCM-SIV with asymmetric key wrapping (RSA-OAEP or ECDH) | Prevent plaintext key leakage in storage and backups | Sample wrap/unwrap logs and successful cryptographic unit test |
| Remote attestation | Support for remote attestation (where available) for on‑prem HSMs | Ensure firmware/trustworthiness of HSMs | Attestation report and verification steps |
| API compatibility | REST/gRPC with documented auth (mTLS or signed requests) and idempotent key operations | Operational reliability and automatable flows | Completed API smoke tests and example clients |
| Key lifecycle controls | Programmatic rotate, revoke, disable, and staged rollout with rollback window | Reduce blast radius and enable safe rotation | Rotation playbook runbook and automated test artifacts |
| Audit logging | Immutable audit trail exportable to SIEM with timestamps, actor, and operation | For compliance and incident forensics | Exported log sample and retention config |
| Latency and availability | 99.95% availability for KMS path and <50 ms median wrap/unwrap in region (hosted) | Prevents inference latency regressions | Synthetic latency tests and SLA statement |
| Network and trust boundary | TLS 1.3, mTLS for HSM control channel, IP allowlist for management plane | Network-level defense in depth | Network policy manifests and firewall rules |

Integration patterns (recommended):
1) Cloud KMS as CMEK (preferred for cloud VPC private deploys)
   - Use KMS to protect a locally generated data encryption key (DEK). Store the wrapped DEK in the deployment secret store.
   - Example: Generate DEK on the host, call KMS: Encrypt(DEK) -> store wrapped key.

2) HSM-backed key store (preferred for high compliance or on‑prem air‑gapped sites)
   - Keys never leave the HSM. Perform wrap/unwrap and asymmetric ops inside the HSM.
   - Use an HSM client that supports local caching of public material but not private key export.

3) Hybrid (HSM for master key, soft-DEKs for operational performance)
   - Master keys in HSM; DEKs generated locally and wrapped by HSM. Use a cache TTL and enable secure rotation.

Network and IAM constraints:
- Management plane (control signals for wrap/unwrap/rotate): must be restricted to operator CIDR ranges and require mTLS client certs.
- Runtime nodes performing wrapping should authenticate with per-node mTLS certs or short-lived workload tokens (OIDC-based).
- Minimum IAM roles and privileges principle-of-least-privilege: separate roles for encryption, decryption, and key administration.

Key rotation and emergency revocation policy:
- Rotation frequency: default 90 days for DEKs; 1–3 years for master keys depending on compliance requirements.
- Staged rotation steps:
  1. Create new key version in KMS/HSM (do not enable immediately).
  2. Deploy runtime code supporting dual-key unwrap for a transition window.
  3. Generate new DEKs and rewrap artifacts incrementally.
  4. Monitor error rates and rollback if >1% increase in crypto errors across nodes within 30 minutes.
  5. Enable new key as primary, deprecate old key after retention window and proof of rewrap completion.
- Emergency revocation: Revoke master key -> system should immediately fail closed for any operations requiring the master key; field engineers to follow the Emergency Key Revocation runbook (Steps below).

Validation and onboarding checklist (pre-install, install, post-install):
Pre-install (customer and field):
- Confirm KMS/HSM certification level and provide attestation.
- Exchange mTLS client certs and bootstrap root CA fingerprints.
- Agree on network ACLs, IP allowlists, and ports (TLS 1.3 only).
- Verify key naming conventions and rotation windows.

Install (operator):
1. Confirm connectivity: curl -v --cert client.pem --key client.key https://kms.example.internal/healthz
2. Perform wrap/unwrap smoke test: generate local DEK, call Encrypt/Decrypt, verify plaintext equals original.
3. Check audit flush: request last 200 audit events and validate operation fields.
4. Run synthetic latency test (1000 ops) and assert median <50ms.

Post-install (validation):
- Run resilience tests: simulate KMS outage and confirm application fallback policy (cache usage) keeps critical operations for configured TTL, then observe graceful degradation.
- Confirm rotation process using canary tenants: rotate keys for a small tenant and validate end-to-end decryption.
- Provide onboarding report with evidence artifacts to security and customer success.

Day-2 operations and monitoring guidance:
- Monitoring: track wrap/unwrap rate, error rate, median latency, and audit log export success. Alerts:
  - P1: unwrap error rate >0.5% sustained 5 min -> Pager to oncall (SRE and field lead)
  - P1: Audit log export failure for 10 min -> Pager
  - P2: median unwrap latency >150ms for 5 min -> Slack alert to infra channel
- Capacity planning: for high-throughput inference workloads, use DEK caching with strict TTL and an LRU cache size tuned to node memory. Document recommended defaults in runtime config: cache_ttl=300s, cache_max_items=1000.
- Regular exercises: quarterly rotation drills and annual attestation re‑validation.

Rollback and emergency procedures (short checklist):
1. If a new key introduces unrecoverable errors, immediately mark the new key version as disabled in KMS/HSM.
2. Force all nodes to use previous wrapped DEKs from backup manifest.
3. If key compromise suspected: rotate master key in HSM, run full rewrap for persisted artifacts, and notify legal/compliance per incident policy.
4. Record and export full audit trail before any destructive actions; preserve evidence for forensic analysis.

Example operational commands and snippets:
- Wrap/unwrap with AWS KMS (example using AWS CLI):
  - Encrypt (wrap DEK): aws kms encrypt --key-id alias/redwood-master --plaintext fileb://dek.bin --output text --query CiphertextBlob > dek.wrapped 
  - Decrypt (unwrap): aws kms decrypt --ciphertext-blob fileb://dek.wrapped --output text --query Plaintext | base64 --decode > dek.bin
- HSM client sample (pseudo):
  - hsm-client gen-key --label=\"rdw-master-v1\" --usage=wrap
  - hsm-client wrap --key=rdw-master-v1 --in=dek.bin --out=dek.wrapped

Operational ownership and SLAs:
- Primary owner: Private Deployments (field engineering) team — contact: field-eng-oncall@redwood.example.com
- Secondary owner: Security Engineering — contact: security-oncall@redwood.example.com
- SLA: KMS control-plane availability 99.95%; customer-specific SLAs to be reflected in the deployment contract addendum.

Documentation and evidence to collect for sign-off:
- KMS/HSM attestation and certs (PDF)
- API smoke test logs and latency reports
- Audit export sample covering onboarding actions
- Rotation acceptance test runbook outputs and canary results

References and appendices:
- Recommended configuration snippet (runtime config YAML example):
  runtime_crypto:
    key_provider: \"kms\"
    provider_endpoint: \"https://kms.example.internal\"
    mTLS_client_cert: \"/etc/redwood/client.pem\"
    wrap_algorithm: \"AES-256-GCM\"
    cache_ttl_seconds: \"300\"

- Related internal pages: see Related Pages metadata at top.

Contacts and escalation ladder:
- Field engineering lead: Diego Ramos (diego@redwood.example.com)
- Security oncall: security-oncall@redwood.example.com
- Cust Success onboarding: onboarding@redwood.example.com

Notes and disclaimers:
- Customers must provide required attestation documents and accept a short maintenance window for initial full rewrap if migrating legacy encrypted assets.
- Where customers cannot provide HSM attestation, field engineering may accept compensating controls (e.g., tamper-evident enclosures and enhanced logging) on a case-by-case basis with Security approval.
